title: Online Therapy Support (Awareness Level)
desc: Understand how online emotional-support services work, what they can and cannot do, and how to stay safe and kind. Awareness only; this is not clinical training.
outcomes: Explain the difference between peer support, coaching and licensed therapy.
Use a safe-contact checklist before joining or recommending a service.
Spot warning signs that need urgent help.
Judge a service for privacy, qualifications and fairness.
Draft a short, kind guide for your community.
task: Produce a one-page safe-use guide for online emotional-support services, with a checklist and an urgent-help card for your place.
condition: A computer or phone, public information, two peers and a mentor. You do not give therapy or advice on treatment in this course.
standard: Guide uses plain words; roles are not mixed up; urgent-help numbers are checked for your place and dated; no diagnosis or treatment advice appears; peers rate Meets or better.
who: Teachers, community leaders, HR staff, volunteers and curious learners.
evidence: guide, checklist, urgent-help card, privacy review
modules: Three kinds of help, and who does what
Understand

People often take a friend, a coach and a therapist to be the same thing. They are not, and mixing them up leads to bad choices. This module gives you a simple map so you can name each kind of help and say what it is for.
Peer support is shared experience between people with no formal training, such as a friends group or a community circle. It gives company and hope, not treatment.
Coaching focuses on goals, habits and skills, such as study routines or a career change. A coach does not diagnose or treat illness.
Therapy is assessment and treatment by a registered professional who is accountable to a recognised body. Only this kind treats mental-health conditions.
When in doubt about which you need, ask a doctor, a school counsellor or a helpline, and say clearly what is happening.

A student feels low for three weeks and has trouble sleeping. Her class group chat is peer support, useful but not treatment. A study coach can help her plan revision. Because the low mood has lasted over two weeks and affects sleep, she books a registered counsellor through her college health centre.
Sort 10 short cases (given by your mentor) into peer support, coaching, therapy or urgent help, and write one sentence of reason for each.
At least 9 of 10 sorted correctly and every reason names what the helper is trained to do.
How online sessions work, step by step
Understand
An online session is a normal appointment that happens through a screen or a phone. Knowing the steps reduces fear and prevents lost sessions.
Steps: find a service, check who runs it, book a time, agree consent and payment, join on time, talk, agree next steps.
Formats: text chat, voice call, video call, or messages left for a reply later. Each suits different people and moods.
Set-up: a private room, headphones, charged device, stable internet, a glass of water and a note of what you want to say.
Fall-back: agree before the session what happens if the line drops, for example a phone call within five minutes.

Imran books a video session for 6 pm. At 5:45 he tests the link, tells his family he needs privacy for an hour, and writes three points on paper. The line drops at 6:20, and the counsellor calls his phone within two minutes as agreed.
Write a pre-session checklist of at least six items and a fall-back plan for a failed connection.
Checklist covers room, device, link test, privacy, notes and fall-back; fall-back names who calls whom and when.
Checking qualifications and honesty
Analyse
Anyone can type "therapist" on a web page. Checking takes ten minutes and protects you or the person you advise.
Look for a named professional, a registration number and the register where it can be checked in your place.
A trustworthy service states its limits, such as that it is not for emergencies, and gives emergency contacts.
Red flags: guaranteed cure, pressure to pay up front for many sessions, no named staff, secret methods.
Record what you checked and the date, because services change.

A site shows registration number 48213. The learner searches the public register for the profession in their country and finds the person, active, with a matching name and city. The site also lists a crisis number. Result: passes. A second site promises "cure anxiety in 3 days" and shows no names. Result: fails.
Check one real or practice service with the checklist and write a half-page finding with sources and the date.
Each check has a source and date; the finding states pass or fail with reasons.
Privacy, consent and data
Evaluate
What you say about your feelings is some of the most private information you have. You should know where it goes.
Ask what is recorded, who can see it, how long it is kept, and whether it can be deleted.
Consent must be clear and can be withdrawn. Children and teenagers may need a guardian too, depending on the place.
Use a private device, a strong password and a locked screen. Do not use a shared or work computer.
Never share another person's story or screenshots without their agreement.

A service keeps session notes for seven years in another country. The learner decides this does not suit them and asks for a service that keeps records locally for a shorter period, then keeps a note of the privacy answers.
Complete a five-question privacy review of one service and record the answers.
All five questions answered from the service's own policy, with the page named.
Warning signs and urgent help
Analyse
Some situations cannot wait for an appointment. Knowing them and acting early can save a life.
Warning signs: talk of wanting to die or self-harm, plans or means, hopelessness, sudden calm after distress, harm to others, abuse, severe confusion.
If someone is in immediate danger, call the local emergency number and stay with them; do not leave them alone.
Ask directly and kindly: "Are you thinking of ending your life?" Asking does not plant the idea.
After the crisis, help the person link to a registered professional and a trusted contact.

A volunteer hears a friend say "I cannot do this any more" and mentions a plan. She stays on the call, asks the question directly, calls the emergency number from a second phone and waits with her friend until help arrives.
Make an urgent-help card with your local emergency number, a crisis line, and three trusted contacts, and check every number.
Numbers verified for your place, dated, and tested by calling a non-emergency number to confirm it exists.
Being a kind helper, within limits
Apply
Good helping is mostly listening. You are not there to fix, diagnose or promise.
Listen first: give full attention, do not interrupt, reflect back what you heard.
Name feelings gently ("That sounds exhausting") and ask what would help.
Do not diagnose, give medicine advice, or promise secrecy you cannot keep when safety is at risk.
Know when to hand over: say "I care about you and I want you to have proper help".
A coach hears a client describe panic attacks. Instead of advising, he says "That sounds frightening. Have you spoken to a doctor?" and offers to help find an appointment.
Role-play two listening conversations of five minutes with a peer and collect their feedback.
Peer reports they felt heard, no advice was forced, and the hand-over sentence was used.
Fairness, cost and access
Evaluate
Help that cannot be reached helps nobody. Language, money, disability and stigma all block people.
Check language options, text-only options, accessible formats and low-cost or free routes such as public clinics or helplines.
Respect culture, faith and gender preferences when matching a helper.
Never pressure anyone to join a service.
Offer to sit with the person while they make the first call.
A community centre lists a free helpline in three languages, a low-cost clinic and a text option for people who cannot talk aloud at home.
List five accessible options for your area and check each one is real.
Each option has a contact, hours, language and cost, and was verified by you.
Write and test your community guide
Create
Bring the course together into one page that a neighbour could use tonight.
Structure: the three kinds of help, the safe-use checklist, the urgent-help card and where to get help in your language.
Use short sentences and large print.
Test with two readers who have not taken the course.
Plan to update the guide every six months.
A school puts the guide on the notice board and asks a teacher to check the numbers each term.
Finish the guide and test it with two readers.
Both readers can say the three kinds of help and where to call in an emergency.
quiz: Name three kinds of help.
Peer support, coaching, licensed therapy. (Covered in module 1: Three kinds of help. To pass that module: At least 9 sorted correctly.)
Does this course teach therapy?
No; awareness only. (Covered in module 2: How online sessions work. To pass that module: Checklist has 6 items.)
How do you check qualifications?
Registration with a recognised body and a public number. (Covered in module 3: Qualifications and honesty. To pass that module: Findings written with the source and date.)
Name one privacy question.
What is recorded, who sees it, how long it is kept. (Covered in module 4: Privacy and consent. To pass that module: Five privacy questions answered.)
What needs urgent help?
Self-harm, harm to others, abuse, severe distress. (Covered in module 5: Warning signs and urgent help. To pass that module: Numbers are verified for your place and dated.)
What do you not do as a helper?
Diagnose or promise outcomes. (Covered in module 6: Being a kind helper. To pass that module: Peer says they felt heard and no advice was forced.)
Why check numbers by date?
Services change. (Covered in module 7: Fairness and access. To pass that module: Each option is checked.)
What is a kind first sentence?
"That sounds hard. What would help?" (Covered in module 8: Write your community guide. To pass that module: Readers can explain it back in their own words.)
Why consider access?
Cost, language or disability can block help. (Covered in module 8: Write your community guide. To pass that module: Readers can explain it back in their own words.)
How often should the guide be updated?
About every 6 months. (Covered in module 8: Write your community guide. To pass that module: Readers can explain it back in their own words.)

ladder: Three kinds of help

L1: learner can name three kinds of help. Focus module: Three kinds of help (Understand, 2 h). People mix up support types. Key points: Peer support: shared experience, no training required. Coaching: goals and habits, not treatment. Licensed therapy: assessment and treatment by a registered professional.

Teach: open with the worked example. A friend group chat is peer support. A career coach helps plan a job change. A registered therapist treats an anxiety disorder. Then set the activity: Sort 10 examples into the three kinds. Mark against the standard: At least 9 sorted correctly. Check at this level: Name three kinds of help. Model answer: Peer support, coaching, licensed therapy. Use everyday examples; stay gentle.
How online sessions work

L2: learner can say why privacy and consent matter. Focus module: How online sessions work (Understand, 2 h). Sessions run by text, voice or video, live or later. Key points: Booking, payment, consent and session rules. Good set-up: quiet room, headphones, stable internet. What to do if the line fails.

Teach: open with the worked example. A learner books a video session, checks the link 10 minutes early and keeps a phone number for backup. Then set the activity: Write a pre-session checklist. Mark against the standard: Checklist has 6 items. Check at this level: Does this course teach therapy? Model answer: No; awareness only. Stress consent.
Qualifications and honesty

L3: learner can use the safe-use checklist. Focus module: Qualifications and honesty (Analyse, 2 h). Anyone can claim to be a helper. Key points: Look for registration with a recognised body and a public number. Check the service explains limits and emergency steps. Be wary of promises to cure fast.

Teach: open with the worked example. A site shows a registration number which the learner checks on the public register. Then set the activity: Check one real or practice service. Mark against the standard: Findings written with the source and date. Check at this level: How do you check qualifications? Model answer: Registration with a recognised body and a public number. Walk through the checklist.
Privacy and consent

L4: learner can run a kind listening chat and hand over. Focus module: Privacy and consent (Evaluate, 2 h). Feelings are private data. Key points: Ask what is recorded, who sees it and how long it is kept. Never share another person's story without consent. Use strong passwords and do not use shared computers.

Teach: open with the worked example. A service keeps notes for 7 years; the learner decides whether that suits them. Then set the activity: Complete a privacy review of one service. Mark against the standard: Five privacy questions answered. Check at this level: Name one privacy question. Model answer: What is recorded, who sees it, how long it is kept. Keep role-plays short and safe.
Warning signs and urgent help

L5: learner can review a service for fairness and privacy. Focus module: Warning signs and urgent help (Analyse, 2 h). Some situations cannot wait. Key points: Thoughts of self-harm, harm to others, abuse or severe distress need urgent human help now. Know your local emergency number and a trusted person. Stay with the person and call; do not leave them alone.

Teach: open with the worked example. A volunteer keeps a card with the local emergency number and a crisis line, checked each month. Then set the activity: Make an urgent-help card. Mark against the standard: Numbers are verified for your place and dated. Check at this level: What needs urgent help? Model answer: Self-harm, harm to others, abuse, severe distress. Show a review of one service.
Fairness and access

L6: learner can coordinate a small volunteer rota. Focus module: Fairness and access (Evaluate, 2 h). Cost, language and disability can block help. Key points: Check language options, accessibility and low-cost routes. Respect cultural and faith differences. Do not push anyone to join.

Teach: open with the worked example. A community lists a free helpline in three languages. Then set the activity: List three accessible options. Mark against the standard: Each option is checked. Check at this level: What do you not do as a helper? Model answer: Diagnose or promise outcomes. Discuss rota and hand-over.
Write your community guide

L7: learner can audit a community guide. Focus module: Write your community guide (Create, 2 h). Pull it together in one page. Key points: Title, three kinds of help, safe-use checklist, urgent-help card. Test with two readers. Update every 6 months.

Teach: open with the worked example. The one-page guide goes on a school notice board with a monthly review date. Then set the activity: Finish and present the guide. Mark against the standard: Readers can explain it back in their own words. Check at this level: Why check numbers by date? Model answer: Services change. Peer audit.
